data.title: Trump says Putin will release diesel onto global market amid unprecedented price surge
data.description: President Donald Trump said Friday that Russian President Vladimir Putin would “immediately” release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel onto the global market. Trump made the announcement on Truth Social and said the action would will help bring diesel prices down. It was not immediately clear how this would work, however, given wide-ranging sanctions that have been applied to Russia since its illegal invasion of Ukraine. Since the start of the Iran war in February, the price of diesel fuel has soared almost 70%, and economists have warned that the price hikes will have wide-ranging inflationary effects on the global economy. In recent weeks, sharp escalations in the Russia-Ukraine war have caused diesel to spike even further, and for multiple weeks the price of diesel set repeated all-time records.

data.title: Elon Musk’s growing SpaceX empire sends AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile shares plunging
data.description: Elon Musk’s plan for SpaceX to “become a major mobile carrier in the U.S.” sent shares of the nation’s big three wireless carriers sliding by double digits Friday, wiping out more than $50 billion in market value before lunch. “Once we receive final FCC approval, Starlink Mobile will deploy a flexible architecture combining our satellite-to-mobile constellation in space with an advanced terrestrial deployment that can seamlessly connect devices everywhere,” the company said late Thursday. It also announced that the Federal Communications Commission had approved the launch of 15,000 new satellites, also under Starlink Mobile, which is a subsidiary of SpaceX. Shares of AT&T and Verizon both dropped 10% on Friday morning, while T-Mobile US stock plunged 14%. Shares of Charter and of Comcast, the parent company of NBC News, also fell throughout the day Friday. Both companies sell wireless services under their own brands using Verizon’s infrastructure. Musk’s empire expands The announcement from SpaceX marked Musk’s latest step to expand his global tech empire. The world’s richest man and its first-ever trillionaire, Musk’s net worth as of Thursday was about $990 billion. Musk’s constellation of companies already includes electric vehicle maker Tesla, the social media site X and xAI, which builds data centers and develops artificial intelligence. SpaceX includes multiple lines of business, too. Starlink sells high-speed internet to companies and consumers worldwide, while Starshield does the same, but to governments. But the major money maker for SpaceX is Starlink, which was worth $2.2 trillion as of Friday. With more than 12 million paying subscribers, Starlink is also the only profitable part of SpaceX’s business, according to its latest earnings report. The acquisition of spectrum was “the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America,” Musk wrote on n X. SpaceX is also a massive U.S. government contractor, building and launching rockets on behalf of NASA and several national security agencies. Favorable decisions by government regulators and additional agency contracts are crucial to maintaining SpaceX’s lofty valuation. White House VIP As a close ally of President Donald Trump and a major donor to his 2024 election effort, Musk is a frequent guest at White House events. At a recent White House state dinner for China’s President Xi Jinping, Musk was seated next to first lady Melania Trump. Just this week, Trump gave Musk an award for achievements in science. As Republicans struggle to hold on to control of the House and Senate in November’s midterm elections, Musk is once again giving tens of millions of dollars to help them. As of Friday, Musk’s America PAC had spent more than $36 million to boost Trump’s fellow Republicans in key battleground races, according to figures compiled by Wired and verified by NBC News. Musk also appears to have support for his deal already from FCC chairman Brendan Carr. “All of this is going to be really good news for the American consumer,” Carr said Friday morning on CNBC. Skeptics on the street Wall Street analysts and Starlink’s potential competitors were skeptical Friday of the SpaceX plan. Absent a deal with an existing wireless carrier, “SpaceX would likely need to build a terrestrial network using macro towers to deliver a user experience on par with traditional wireless carriers,” wrote analysts at JPMorgan Chase. “We continue to see limited near-term risk to U.S. wireless incumbents given the time, infrastructure and capital required to build a competitive terrestrial network,” they added. Put another way, the analysts think SpaceX plan’s does not pose an imminent threat to the established carriers because it takes a lot more than just satellites to deliver reliable wireless service. SpaceX would need earth-based infrastructure to bolster its network of satellites because the radio waves it purchased would likely be unable to reach the interior of some buildings, wrote analysts at UBS. “We still believe it will take time for SpaceX to scale its wireless ambitions.” Like the analysts, the major telecom companies feeling the sting from Musk’s announcement also downplayed any risk that Starlink might pose to their businesses. “Acquisition of spectrum alone does not provide the network or infrastructure to offer true nationwide coverage or to compete with mobile providers,” Verizon said in a statement to NBC News. “A company can have billions of dollars of spectrum, but if they do not have the network to use it, it’s just empty airwaves.” John Saw, president of technology at T-Mobile wrote, “I have tremendous respect for what SpaceX has accomplished in space,” but that building a network would take “years of engineering.” “You can acquire spectrum in a single transaction. You cannot acquire a nationwide, high-performing wireless network overnight,” he wrote on LinkedIn. AT&T did not respond to a request for comment on Friday. The three big wireless companies have a complicated relationship with Starlink. In 2022, T-Mobile announced a partnership with SpaceX, but recently dropped the name of the company from parts of its website. And when the three wireless companies announced a joint venture recently to “eliminate coverage ‘dead zones’ and expand satellite coverage,” there was no mention of SpaceX or Starlink.

data.title: Trump establishes panel to probe Fed governor Lisa Cook in latest attempt to fire her
data.description: President Donald Trump on Friday signed an order directing the attorney general and other top federal officials to establish a committee to investigate Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, in his latest attempt to fire her. “By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the laws of the United States of America, I hereby establish a committee of inquiry (Committee) to investigate allegations that Federal Reserve Governor Lisa D. Cook made false statements in connection with one or more mortgage instruments,” read a presidential memorandum posted to the White House website. It said that the committee would “investigate the allegations against Governor Cook and report to me whether there is “cause for Governor Cook’s removal.” “Governor Cook may submit a written position statement to the Committee regarding the allegations,” the memorandum said. The unprecedented White House announcement comes after a top White House official in August wrote a letter to Cook, saying that Trump was considering removing her from the Federal Reserve board. The White House memorandum said that Cook “shall appear at the hearing and be examined by the Committee” as well as “present argument, written evidence, and written witness statements regarding the evidence and allegations.” The committee is set to meet on November 5 for the hearing, two days after the midterm elections. No president has ever fired a top Fed official. The letter Friday follows a June Supreme Court ruling, which allowed Cook to remain in her job for now. But the justices did not permanently block Trump from removing Cook, instead ruling that she had the right to an opportunity to defend herself. Trump’s latest move stems from allegations first leveled against Cook in August 2025 by Federal Housing Finance Authority chief Bill Pulte. Trump amplified those allegations on social media and, citing a “criminal referral” he said Pulte had sent to the Justice Department, attempted to remove her from the Fed’s board. Pulte alleged that Cook committed mortgage fraud, however documents obtained and reviewed by NBC News later revealed that Cook declared that the property in question was to be used as a “vacation home” and not her primary residence. Cook, a Governor on the Federal Reserve’s Board, has a permanent vote on interest rates. Trump and Pulte’s attacks on Cook came amid a long-running pressure campaign by the administration to get the U.S. central bank to cut interest rates. Throughout the more than year-long battle, Cook has consistently maintained that she did nothing wrong. Just weeks ago, Cook’s lawyer told the White House for a second time that “there is no legal basis for President Trump to remove Governor Cook for cause.” “An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing,” said Abbe Lowell on August 26. “These attacks on Governor Cook are not about real estate paperwork; they are an attempt by President Trump to force the Federal Reserve to bend to his will.” Lowell said he and Cook were prepared to continue to fight “any illegal attempt to remove Governor Cook.” Cook’s legal team did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday about the latest development.

data.title: Trump’s moves to boost diesel supplies have not yet lowered prices
data.description: U.S. diesel prices remain at near record highs, up 70% since the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began despite two high-profile recent moves by President Donald Trump to boost supplies of the fuel: pressuring allies to release emergency reserves and expanding access to tax-exempt red-dyed diesel. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have triggered an unprecedented global fuel supply crunch, pushing average U.S. diesel prices to $6.28 a gallon on Thursday according to AAA. “Aside from a recession that hammers consumption, the only thing that can prevent oil prices from rising further and put them on a sharp downward trajectory is a durable end to conflicts in the Arabian Gulf and between Russia and Ukraine,” said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy Group. “Otherwise, policy options range from marginal to counterproductive.” High fuel prices have made it harder for Trump and his Republican Party to defend narrow congressional majorities in the November 3 midterm elections. The cost of living is the top item cited by voters in a Reuters/Ipsos poll, and high diesel prices put particular pressure on traditional Republican constituencies: farmers, truckers and rural voters. Trump’s approval rating is at a record-low 32%, according to the poll. The administration has touted a G7 agreement to release 100 million barrels of oil and petroleum products as a major step to help ease prices, but those barrels appear to largely cover what remains of a March emergency release by International Energy Agency members, rather than new supply. A White House official disputed that characterization, saying the earlier commitments were not specifically for refined products. The administration negotiated for the previously committed barrels to be front-loaded with diesel and released on a tight timeline beginning immediately, the official said. The White House said Trump was focused on easing temporary disruptions while pursuing longer-term energy policies. The administration’s other major initiative, an executive order allowing red-dyed diesel on public roads through year-end, has drawn limited industry uptake. The fuel is chemically identical to what trucks normally burn but is tinted to show it is exempt from the 24.4-cent-per-gallon federal highway tax. The order defers the federal tax and waives penalties for burning off-road fuel on highways. But major retailers and marketers remain wary of selling it because of unclear tax liabilities, logistical hurdles and the risk of fines when trucks cross state lines. The tax savings are relatively small with diesel prices above $6 a gallon. David Fialkov, president of NATSO, which represents truck stops and travel centers, said the White House appeared to be encouraging the supply chain to sell dyed fuel through channels not traditionally used for highway diesel, but said most reputable retailers and marketers were unlikely to do so. John Tirado, president of New Jersey-based commercial fuel supplier Summa Energy, called the red-dyed diesel plan “a Band-Aid on a much bigger problem.” The White House says more than 4,000 retailers distribute dyed diesel. It said Treasury Department guidance will clarify the rules, allowing drivers to use it without federal tax or penalty. It says the savings should outweigh any detour costs for truckers seeking out the fuel. “The fundamental problem facing the U.S. is not taxation but an exceptionally tight global market for refined products,” said Caspian Conran, lead economist at Baringa, citing disruptions to energy flows from the Middle East and reduced refining output elsewhere. He described the measures as short-term steps ahead of the election that could provide “probably a few weeks of relief,” rather than a durable solution.

data.title: South Korea and Japan are buffeted by hacks as AI lowers bar for cybercriminals
data.description: South Korean and Japanese companies are racing to strengthen cyber defenses after a wave of attacks that cybersecurity experts say are highlighting how AI may be lowering the bar for criminals with limited technical skills. Nine South Korean banks and two mega-churches are investigating cyberattacks that may have involved AI tools, while Japanese companies including Daiwa Securities, SoftBank and the Lawson convenience store chain have been hit by a recent surge in cyber incidents. Authorities are still investigating whether and how AI was used in many of the breaches. But cybersecurity specialists say the technology is helping attackers automate tasks from scanning for software vulnerabilities to crafting phishing campaigns, making cybercrime faster, cheaper and harder to detect. “AI doesn’t get tired ... My view is that Japan is essentially being subjected to carpet bombing,” said Nobuo Miwa, president of the Tokyo-based cybersecurity firm S&J Corp. Japan recorded more cybersecurity incidents in the first nine months of the year than in all of last year, according to data from TrendAI. Incidents rose to 86 in September, up about 18% from August and 37% from July. The rise suggests attackers have crossed a threshold in “effort, motivation and technical capability,” while AI has largely erased language and other barriers that once hindered foreign hackers, Miwa said. U.S. cybersecurity company CrowdStrike said a 26-year-old China-based attacker suspected of being behind the South Korean bank incidents would probably not have been able to carry out the campaign without AI assistance. The individual, whom CrowdStrike assessed was pursuing financial gain, used a Chinese-developed AI agent and Anthropic’s Claude Code, according to the company. “While (the hacker’s) capabilities were not terribly sophisticated, they were effective,” said Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike’s senior vice president of counter adversary operations. AI-powered tools are also making it harder for defenders to spot suspicious behavior, said Choi Kyoungjin, director of the Center for AI, Data and Policy at Gachon University near Seoul. “With general-purpose AI models, even ordinary users with malicious intent can ask the system to look for vulnerabilities and it will do much of that work for them,” he said. South Korea reported 1,236 cyber incidents in the first half of the year, up 20% from a year earlier. While server hacking cases fell, reports of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks and ransomware rose 56.7% and 76.8%, respectively, according to government data. The South Korean bank incidents underscore the need for stronger security controls and more rigorous testing as AI evolves, Meyers said. “The genie is out of the bottle, so to speak.” Although the breaches have not yet resulted in material financial losses, risks could increase if stolen data is used in phishing or similar text-message “smishing” campaigns, Karen Wu, senior analyst at Fitch, wrote in a note. “We expect the incidents to result in regulatory penalties, customer compensation costs, and a sector-wide increase in cybersecurity spending,” Wu said. Warnings about AI’s growing role in cybercrime are increasingly coming from the technology’s developers. Anthropic and Alphabet’s Google have both warned that AI-assisted attacks are becoming more common globally. “At this point, we can assume that all threat actors are using AI in some capacity and their operations have benefited,” John Hultquist, the chief analyst at Google’s Threat Intelligence Group, said last month. Regulators in Japan and South Korea have begun responding. South Korea’s Financial Services Commission has directed financial industry associations, regulators and affected executives to complete a 12-point cybersecurity self-assessment. In Japan, digital transformation minister Toshiharu Furukawa convened a meeting of ministries and agencies on Thursday following the recent attacks. The National Cybersecurity Office plans to issue warnings to businesses. S&J’s Miwa said he expected elevated levels of cyberattacks to persist. “The attackers have experienced a breakthrough that has rendered many of the old assumptions obsolete,” he said. “Our defenses need their own breakthrough as well.”

data.title: In new Elon Musk documentary, his lieutenants are the most damning voices
data.description: SAN RAFAEL, Calif. — It’s easy to find people with bad things to say about tech magnate Elon Musk, and plenty of those people show up in “Musk,” a new documentary about his rise to political and corporate power. What’s more surprising in the film are the unflattering statements by some of his own employees, including ones who still work for him. Some of the harshest scenes in the film, which opens Friday in Los Angeles and New York, are ones in which Musk’s lieutenants were recorded on video or in audio as they wielded power on his behalf or discussed what they had already done for him. Warning: This article includes spoilers for the documentary “Musk.” There are clips of Ashok Elluswamy, a high-ranking Tesla engineer, acknowledging in a videotaped deposition that an infamous hype video he helped put together in 2016 about the company’s self-driving capabilities was not an accurate representation of Tesla’s technology at the time. There are also audio snippets from Jared Birchall, who handles Musk’s personal matters. He is heard on a recording of a phone call with online influencer Ashley St. Clair, shortly after she had given birth to a child she and Musk conceived, in which he plays hardball on child support arrangements. Both incidents were documented in the media: Reuters reported in 2023 on the transcript of Elluswamy’s deposition, and The Wall Street Journal reported last year on Birchall’s phone call with St. Clair. But the video and the audio appear to be newly public, giving the documentary a mix of voices beyond the usual critics and creating moments of surprise even for a viewer who is familiar with the ins and outs of Musk’s complicated story. Filmmaker Alex Gibney says in the documentary that he and his team spent more than three years researching Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, pulling together not only archival interviews and hard-to-find footage but also a database of quotes from Musk that are peppered throughout the film. Musk, 55, did not participate in the documentary, and he has panned it, saying on X that it is a “hit piece” and that Gibney has “zero integrity.” Musk, Tesla, SpaceX, Elluswamy and Birchall did not respond to requests for comment. The nearly four-hour film is a comprehensive tour through Musk’s life story, with deep dives into the growth of SpaceX and Tesla, his fathering of 14 known children and his on-again, off-again alliance with President Donald Trump, including his becoming the biggest donor to Trump’s 2024 campaign. The film is a reminder of how often Musk has put himself at the center of public discourse and pop culture, and it moves swiftly through the highlights and lowlights: from his 2021 hosting gig on “Saturday Night Live” and his chaotic purchase of Twitter the next year to his Grok chatbot’s embracing the identity “MechaHitler” and his wielding of a chain saw early in Trump’s second term. “I like to call it a ‘svelte’ four-hour film,” producer Jessie Deeter said at a screening Wednesday at the Mill Valley Film Festival in Marin County, California. (The film has a 10-minute intermission, but it is still roughly the length of the 1962 epic “Lawrence of Arabia.”) At the screening, which was about 90% full, the biggest applause came during a moment of anti-Musk defiance, as a former career federal employee explained why they quit the Trump administration last year rather than cooperate with Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. The film lands at another potentially pivotal moment for Musk, amid speculation that Democrats may investigate him if they take control of Congress after the midterm elections. Polling shows that Musk remains deeply divisive, with a majority of Americans holding unfavorable views of him even as Trump honored him at the White House on Thursday. The documentary demonstrates that Musk’s dabbling in politics is nothing new: Archival videos show that, years before he endorsed Trump in 2024, Musk was rubbing elbows with politicians such as former California Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, and the late Sen. Dianne Feinstein, D-Calif., and getting benefits in return, such as low-emission credits for Tesla. Part of what drives the documentary forward is how it crosses genres: Parts of it feel like a political thriller or a legal whodunit, while others are like a video game simulation, a science fiction fantasy or a celebrity tabloid drama. Other moments are closer to a horror film, especially as Gibney narrates some of the graphic details of collisions involving Tesla’s driver-assistance software. He includes, for example, dashcam video from a 2019 crash in which a Tesla on “Autopilot” ran a stop sign in Florida and killed a pedestrian — a crash for which a jury found Tesla 33% at fault and ordered it to pay $243 million in damages. One of the people interviewed in the film, science fiction author and tech activist Cory Doctorow, adds to the grim feeling by wearing a guillotine pin on his lapel. Later, the documentary lingers again on death, as Gibney tries to tally the human cost of Musk’s drive last year to dismantle the U.S. Agency for International Development. Between shots of malnourished children in Africa and elsewhere, Samantha Power, who was a USAID administrator during the Biden administration, says the cuts froze some food programs for the world’s poor and blames the cuts for 14 million potential deaths. (The number is based on a projection published last year estimating possible deaths over the following five years.) In the film’s rendering, the horror of those statistics and images stands in stark contrast with Musk’s ongoing obsession: traveling deeper into space, including to Mars, for the potential benefit of future, unborn generations. A few parts of the film are presented without evidence or explanation. Gibney boosts a conspiracy theory that Musk used his Starlink constellation of internet satellites to meddle in the 2024 election — an unfounded idea that independent fact-checkers have long criticized. He also raises concerns about potential data collection by Starlink satellites and by Tesla vehicles but does not go beyond vague theories. A more pressing question the film wrestles with is whether or how much Musk has changed over his years in the public spotlight. The film repeatedly shows a younger Musk who is not only physically different, with thinner hair and a slighter build, but also speaking about different issues from those he addresses now — including “oil addiction,” an old motivation behind growing Tesla. Another of Musk’s associates, former SpaceX engineer Jim Cantrell, says in the film that Musk has changed less than some people may imagine. “Success has allowed him to take the lid off what he’s really thinking,” he says.

data.title: Inflation and tariffs push U.S. holiday spending projections to a record $1.7 trillion
data.description: Americans are projected to spend more money than ever this holiday season. But that’s not necessarily because they will be giving more gifts or spreading more good cheer.

data.title: Trump awards Musk and other tech titans National Medals of Science
data.description: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump joined some of America’s most powerful tech leaders Thursday at a summit the White House billed as the start of a “golden age” of American science. Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, AMD CEO Lisa Su, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Dell founder Michael Dell gathered with Trump and a host of administration officials and scientific luminaries for the Science: A New Golden Age Summit at the United States Institute of Peace. “We live in an age of American wonders and technological marvels, and with the help of the brilliant men and women here today, we will always be on top,” Trump said. Trump awarded the National Medal of Science to Musk, Brin, Huang and Su. He awarded the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Nadella and Dell. Trump presented each of the awardees with medals and a certificate of honor, later asking some of the awardees’ families to join him on stage to take photos. “You’re going to go down in the annals of history as being great,” Trump told the awardees. “The Trump Administration is grateful for the contributions of these incredible leaders in science and technology. These recipients are helping ensure America keeps leading the world in innovation,” White House spokesperson Liz Huston said in a statement. The celebration took place just hours after Vice President JD Vance announced that the Trump administration would suspend Microsoft, whose CEO was a guest of honor at the event, and several other companies from a program that allows foreign workers to apply for green cards. Several of the summit’s speakers emphasized the importance of immigrants to America’s scientific power. “I was an immigrant, and my parents brought us here to pursue the American dream,” Huang told NBC News, as he walked through the venue with his parents. “It’s an incredible honor, and something that could only happen here in America,” he said of receiving the award. Carnegie Mellon University president Farnam Jahanian highlighted the importance of a welcoming immigration system in a conversation about the future of American research universities. Jahanian pointed out that China produces more engineers and scientists than the U.S., Europe and Japan put together. “We need to have an immigration policy that can recruit the best talent to come to this country, speaking as an immigrant who has benefited from the opportunities this country has,” Jahanian said. “It’s important to recruit the best talent to come here, so they stay here and contribute,” he said. An all-day affair meant to highlight the American scientific enterprise, the Summit built on a July report from Office of Science and Technology Policy head Michael Kratsios about how the Trump Administration aims to reinvigorate scientific discovery and innovation. “This is the golden age,” Trump said, taking the stage to kick off the celebration’s afternoon program. “We are an extremely high I.Q. audience, for a change,” Trump said, drawing chuckles from the audience. The Science: A New Golden Age report, and Thursday’s gathering, aim to tackle what the White House sees as growing scientific bureaucracy and stagnating innovation. Kratsios highlighted the ballooning costs of clinical trials and falling rates of novel drugs approved for patient use as examples of increased scientific sluggishness. The report says the administration will streamline funding to promising scientists instead of routing funding through established institutions. The event kicked off with a series of announcements about funding for new scientific initiatives, including a pledge of around $2.4 billion of AI computing credits and scientific tools by America’s leading AI companies for federal agencies working on a variety of scientific issues prioritized by the White House. The areas include quantum algorithms, AI-driven physical laboratories and improving the efficiency of nuclear engineering. Kratsios also presided over an announcement between NASA administrator Jared Isaacman and Energy Secretary Chris Wright of a new partnership to embrace nuclear technology in space exploration. “Thanks to President Trump, America’s nuclear renaissance is reaching a new frontier,” Wright said. Isaacman said that nuclear power would allow NASA spacecraft to travel farther and operate for longer periods of time, “opening an entirely new frontier for exploration and discovery.” The day focused on a handful of scientific fields, including artificial intelligence — now referred to as “super intelligence” by the Trump administration — nuclear power, quantum computing and metascience, or the study of science itself. “Super intelligence is going to be the biggest unlock for scientists,” Kratsios said, opening the celebration. Representatives from America’s leading AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Amazon Web Services, and Micron Technology took the stage to announce their new partnerships with the federal government. A variety of scientists from academic institutions and companies gave a series of lightning talks about their research, which largely focused on nuclear energy and the use of AI to accelerate their research. The speakers oscillated between using “AI” and “SI” — the term preferred by administration officials since Trump issued an executive order renaming the technology. John Martinis, a professor of physics at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and recipient of the Nobel Prize in physics, said the technology was already accelerating his group’s research. Asked what a golden age of science would look like to him, Martinis said he didn’t have to look far. “I feel like we’re in it right now,” he said. “It’s really exciting what’s happening with SI.”

data.title: Starbucks says it’s focused on turnaround after report it explored Chipotle merger
data.description: Wall Street was buzzing Thursday about a possible merger that would amount to much more than a hill of beans. Starbucks said it was focused on its turnaround plan, following a report in the Financial Times saying the coffee house chain explored a potential deal to take over Chipotle Mexican Grill. “Our team is laser-focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy,” Starbucks said in a statement. “We have strong momentum and confidence in our long-term growth potential.” The company added that it typically doesn’t comment on what it described as “rumors and speculation” and that it looks forward to sharing its next earnings results later in October. Starbucks’ comment came after the FT reported that Starbucks had hired advisers in recent months to work on a takeover proposal for Chipotle. NBC News has not confirmed the report. A tie-up between the two companies would mean a massive shakeup in the restaurant industry, which is grappling with consumers changing their spending and eating habits. Before the report emerged, sending shares of Chipotle higher by 6.2%, the company had a total market value of about $39 billion. For comparison, Starbucks’ market value stands at more than $105 billion. Chipotle did not return a request for comment on Thursday afternoon. A deal between the two companies would also reunite CEO Brian Niccol with the company he led before he jumped to Starbucks in 2024. Investors appeared worried that a deal could be a distraction for Niccol and his company, though. Starbucks shares fell as much as 6.6% Thursday, but closed the day only slightly lower. The company is in the midst of a wide-ranging turnaround plan engineered by Niccol, including a redesign of Starbucks stores, new service standards to speed up customers’ orders, a refreshed menu, and a reboot for its rewards program. Just weeks ago, Niccol touted the plan’s results, saying “tremendous progress” has been made. Shareholders have seen promising returns too. For the year, Starbucks shares are up almost 11%. That closely tracks with the S&P 500’s 13% return so far this year. The company has also far outperformed the negative 6.7% return that the S&P 500 Consumer Discretionary sector has seen this year. Chipotle shares have sagged by more than 11% this year and more than 20% over the last 12 months. In July, the company’s latest earnings results beat expectations but that followed a period of slow traffic and price hikes. Those results also came alongside soaring gas prices for consumers. “We’re seeing encouraging progress because we’re focused on the right growth drivers,” Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said in a statement in July. Like Starbucks, Chipotle has also revamped its rewards program and has made tweaks to its menu to lure customers back. Chipotle has also started expanding outside of the U.S., with plans to open stores in Mexico, South Korea and Saudi Arabia.

data.title: Microsoft is being suspended from program to apply for green cards for H-1B visa workers, Vance says
data.description: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump’s administration is suspending tech giant Microsoft from a program to apply for green cards for workers who come to the U.S. to live and work using an H-1B visa as it accuses the company of fraud. “If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” said Vice President JD Vance in a White House news conference announcing the decision. The H-1B program has long been a target of Trump supporters who say that the program undercuts American workers and is rife with abuse. H-1B visas are meant for high-skilled jobs that are difficult to find American workers to fill. Technology companies are the biggest users, with nearly three-quarters of approvals going to workers from India. Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Vance announcement came one day after Trump’s Republican administration launched another broadside against international students and their ability to work in the U.S. The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States. The proposed rule would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the Optional Practice Training program, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school. Vance also called out universities that he suggested were abusing a program to allow international students to come to the U.S. These temporary visas, called J-1 visas, allow international visitors to temporarily come to the U.S. for work and study exchange programs. Vance singled out nine universities that he said merited further investigation for J-1 visa fraud, saying they used the program in greater proportions than their counterparts.
